title: Measuring Management Across Nations
text:
In the early 2000s the economists Nicholas Bloom and John Van Reenen set out to measure something many economists had assumed could not be measured: the quality of management. With a team of interviewers, they phoned plant managers at more than seven hundred medium-sized manufacturing firms in the United States, Britain, France and Germany.

Instead of asking managers to rate themselves, the interviewers asked open questions, such as what happens when a problem is found on the production line, how targets are set, and how good and bad performers are treated. They then scored the answers against a set of basic practices covering monitoring, targets and incentives.

The scores varied enormously, both between firms and between countries, with American firms on average scoring highest. Better management scores were clearly associated with higher productivity, profits and growth. Two patterns stood out. Firms facing strong competition were better managed. And family-owned firms in which control had passed to the eldest son, rather than to a professional manager chosen on merit, were much more often badly run.
lesson: Simple management practices like clear targets, regular monitoring and rewarding real performance matter. Choose leaders by ability, not by birthright.
source: Bloom, N., and Van Reenen, J. (2007). Measuring and explaining management practices across firms and countries. Quarterly Journal of Economics, 122(4), 1351-1408.
caveat: The cross-country findings show associations, not proof that practices cause the performance differences.
